section_summary: This section concerns Japanese petroleum supply, distribution, and efforts to develop domestic fuels. Company reports describe Japan’s growing share of the North China oil trade and restrictions on foreign competitors; diplomatic reports examine Japan’s new petroleum sales monopoly, synthetic oil production, and aviation gasoline projects. Other documents address Japanese oil activity in Mexico and the possible effects of American export restrictions.

subfiles.title: Petroleum in the Dutch East Indies
subfiles.about: A steamship manager alleges Standard Oil misinforms Americans about Japan because of Dutch East Indies oil interests.
subfiles.summary: Points to a Justice Department letter containing M. Higashikuze’s allegation.

subfiles.title: Petroleum rigs ordered for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese order for ten rigs from Wilson Manufacturing Company.
subfiles.summary: References Walden’s letter on ten rigs reportedly ordered by Japanese buyers.

subfiles.title: High-octane gasoline for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese efforts to buy high-octane gasoline through a South American channel.
subfiles.summary: References a confidential telegram reporting difficulty obtaining high-octane gasoline.

subfiles.title: Japanese petroleum situation
subfiles.about: References photostatic reports concerning Japan’s petroleum situation.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to a Justice Department letter transmitting reports.

subfiles.title: Proposed Suez–Cairo pipeline
subfiles.to: Officer in charge, American Mission, Cairo
subfiles.about: Transmits an intercepted Shell communication and requests information about a proposed Egyptian pipeline.
subfiles.summary: Encloses a censorship intercept and requests a report on the proposed Suez–Cairo pipeline.

subfiles.title: Japanese share of North China petroleum imports
subfiles.doc_type: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum
subfiles.about: Summarizes statistics showing rapid Japanese gains in North China petroleum imports.
subfiles.summary: Notes rising Japanese shares of kerosene, gasoline, lubricating oil, and diesel imports.

subfiles.title: Japanese Oil Development
subfiles.from: A. H. Elliot, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Provides regional statistics and a report on Japanese petroleum trade and installations in North China.
subfiles.summary: The company reports sharply increased Japanese market shares in the Yangtze Valley, Shandong, and Tianjin territories through November 1939. It describes storage facilities serving Japanese military and commercial needs, permits and shipment restrictions burdening foreign firms, and price and exchange policies favoring Japanese suppliers. It warns that Japan is building a foundation for dominance of North China petroleum markets.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Japanese petroleum statistics
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the company’s statistics on Japanese petroleum imports into China.
subfiles.summary: Thanks Elliot for the detailed data.

subfiles.title: Gasoline export contracts for Japan
subfiles.about: References a conversation about alleged violations of gasoline export contracts involving Japanese agencies and Americans.
subfiles.summary: Points to a memorandum of the Japanese ambassador’s conversation with Secretary Hull.

subfiles.title: Japanese monopoly for petroleum sales: departmental précis
subfiles.doc_type: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Tokyo report on Japan’s new monopoly for petroleum distribution and sales.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes the proposed national and prefectural sales companies, foreign firms’ negotiations to preserve separate brands, and retailer opposition. It finds no immediate need for American action.

subfiles.title: Japanese Monopoly for the Sale of Petroleum Products
subfiles.from: W. Garland Richardson, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Explains Japan’s new petroleum distribution monopoly and its effects on foreign suppliers and retailers.
subfiles.summary: The report traces the replacement of wholesalers by a national sales company and prefectural sales companies after February 1, 1940. American and British firms resist product mixing and loss of brand identity while negotiating separate storage and branded retail sales. It also discusses lubricating oil exemptions, quotas, reduced retailer margins, and opposition that could undermine the system.

subfiles.title: Restrictions on American petroleum products in North China
subfiles.about: References restrictions on moving and selling American petroleum products in several North China localities.
subfiles.summary: Points to an enclosure concerning Fengzhen, Suiyuan, Kalgan, and Baoding.

subfiles.title: File note on Standard-Vacuum letter
subfiles.about: Notes that Standard-Vacuum supplied the Department with a copy of its letter directly.
subfiles.summary: Suggests reading the previously supplied copy.

subfiles.title: Reading instruction for covering despatch
subfiles.about: Directs attention to the covering despatch and first two pages of its enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Requests review of the despatch and opening enclosure pages.

subfiles.title: Japanese Petroleum Activities in North China
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards company correspondence and a report on Japanese petroleum activity in North China.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits a Yokohama company letter, its Shanghai report and blueprint, and the Embassy’s acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum letter on Japanese petroleum activities
subfiles.from: C. E. Meyer, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Sends a Shanghai report and blueprint and warns of Japanese oil traders’ councils in China.
subfiles.summary: Meyer says Japanese firms’ proposed councils to control supplies and prices threaten established American oil interests.

subfiles.title: Japanese Oil Development in North China
subfiles.from: F. J. Twogood, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company, Shanghai
subfiles.about: Details Japanese petroleum sales, installations, and trade advantages across North China.
subfiles.summary: Regional tables track Japanese commercial shipments of kerosene, gasoline, lubricants, and diesel from 1936 through November 1939. The report describes new depots at Gough Island, Pukou, and Qingdao and argues that permits, transport controls, fixed prices, and currency arrangements disadvantage foreign importers. It concludes that Japan may come to dominate North China’s petroleum markets.

subfiles.title: Embassy acknowledgment of Standard-Vacuum report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Meyer’s letter and promises to forward the North China oil report to Washington.
subfiles.summary: Thanks Meyer and confirms forwarding of the material.

subfiles.title: Japanese oil activities in Mexico
subfiles.about: References an investigation of Japanese oil activities and a crude oil sales contract in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Points to a despatch and contract concerning Japanese purchases of Mexican crude.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities in the Mexican Oil Industry and Proposed Trans-Isthmian Pipeline
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Transmits investigations of Japanese oil interests, Mexican concessions, a proposed pipeline, and crude purchases.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reviews rumors of Japanese participation in Mexican oil ventures and a pipeline across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec. It encloses investigative reports and a summary of a contract for Mexican crude sold to Japanese interests.

subfiles.title: Investigation of Japanese oil interests in Mexico
subfiles.about: Investigates Japanese-linked companies, concessions, and drilling operations in the Mexican oil industry.
subfiles.summary: The report identifies Japanese involvement in a Mexican crude purchase and examines concessions held or transferred among local oil companies in Veracruz and Tamaulipas. It lists drilling obligations and describes several wells, equipment purchases, and uneven progress in the field.

subfiles.title: Proposed trans-isthmian oil pipeline
subfiles.about: Assesses reported plans for oil transport across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec.
subfiles.summary: The investigator describes tank and transport works and finds little firm evidence that a pipeline is under construction.

subfiles.title: Summary of Mexican crude oil sale contract
subfiles.about: Summarizes terms for a sale of Mexican crude oil to Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: Lists quantity, delivery, pricing, discount, and payment provisions; the OCR obscures several figures.

subfiles.title: Revised petroleum statistics for Japan
subfiles.about: Introduces revised estimates of Japan’s petroleum position and supersedes an earlier memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Says revised information leaves earlier conclusions unchanged.

subfiles.title: Japan’s dependence on American aviation gasoline
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s reliance on American aviation fuel, blending materials, and crude oil.
subfiles.summary: Young judges Japan heavily dependent on U.S. supplies of high-octane gasoline, tetraethyl lead, iso-octane, and suitable crude. He distinguishes those needs from lower-grade fuels available elsewhere and estimates that existing stocks could sustain Japan’s war in China for at least another year if American supplies stopped.

subfiles.title: Progress of synthetic petroleum manufacture in Japan
subfiles.doc_type: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Tokyo despatch and attaché report on Japanese synthetic oil production.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum distinguishes a small Miike pilot plant from a larger Nippon Yuka operation and describes government subsidies and production targets. It stresses continued dependence on foreign equipment and oil supplies, especially high-pressure cylinders obtainable from the United States.

subfiles.title: Manufacture of Synthetic Petroleum
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese claims of synthetic oil success and encloses an attaché’s assessment.
subfiles.summary: Grew recounts press claims about the Miike plant, the Fischer process, and additional planned plants. The enclosed assessment finds Japan far from petroleum independence because output remains limited and construction depends on foreign equipment.

subfiles.title: Status of Japan’s artificial petroleum industry
subfiles.about: Evaluates Japanese coal liquefaction plants, subsidies, targets, and reliance on imported industrial equipment.
subfiles.summary: Smith considers Mitsui’s Miike unit a pilot plant and reports that Nippon Yuka has already produced synthetic oil. He details state funding and ambitious gasoline and heavy-oil targets but doubts large-scale completion given shortages of money, equipment, and materials. He concludes that restrictions on American high-pressure cylinders would seriously hamper the industry.

subfiles.title: Petroleum Distribution in Japan
subfiles.doc_type: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum
subfiles.from: Iven B. White, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Provides background for possible Tidewater Associated–Mitsubishi negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes foreign and Japanese oil companies, Mitsubishi’s relationship with Tidewater Associated, and Japan’s national and prefectural joint sales system. It explains foreign firms’ successful efforts to retain separate storage and branding. It then considers reduced consumption, possible crude imports from the Dutch East Indies, and exchange restrictions affecting remittances.

subfiles.title: Cover note on aviation gasoline export restrictions
subfiles.about: Introduces a Yokohama consular letter on the effect of a moral embargo on Japan’s gasoline program.
subfiles.summary: Calls attention to Shelton’s estimate of the embargo’s effects.

subfiles.title: Developments in Japan’s Self-Sufficiency Program in the Production of Aviation Gasoline
subfiles.from: Iven B. White, American Vice Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports an engineer’s assessment of export restrictions on Japanese iso-octane projects.
subfiles.summary: George E. Shelton says the loss of American supervision will delay Mitsubishi’s plant and leave Nippon Oil’s less advanced plant without a clear completion date. He argues that Japan lacks specialized equipment and some basic materials needed to build larger iso-octane plants, so an export embargo would sharply curtail its aviation gasoline program.

subfiles.title: Developments in Japan’s Self-Sufficiency Program in the Production of Aviation Gasoline (duplicate copy)
subfiles.from: Iven B. White, American Vice Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Repeats the preceding letter on delays and material shortages affecting Japanese iso-octane plants.
subfiles.summary: A second copy records Shelton’s estimates of delays to Mitsubishi and Nippon Oil projects and the likely impact of an American export embargo.
